items.prompt: The writer says the leaves were laid like the tiles on a roof. Why?

options.text: to show that the stall had a real roof
options.why: The stall had nothing to cover the fruit.

options.text: to show that the leaves overlapped to keep the rain out
to show that the leaves were red
options.why: Banana leaves are green, and the colour is not the point.

options.text: to show that the leaves were heavy
options.why: Tiles on a roof are about covering, not weight.

hints: Think about how tiles sit on a roof.
Each tile sits a little over the next one.
What do the tiles on a roof stop from getting in?
items.explanation: Roof tiles overlap so that rain runs off. The writer uses this comparison to show the leaves covered the fruit in the same way.

items.prompt: Put the events of the story in order.
items: Dark clouds rolled over the hills.
Dewi spotted the pile of banana leaves.
They covered the fruit with the leaves.
hints: Find each event in the story.
Stories are told in the order that things happen.
Start with the first thing that went wrong on that Saturday.
items.explanation: The clouds came first. Then Dewi saw the leaves and they covered the fruit. The rain fell, and afterwards a lady bought mangoes.

items.prompt: In this text, what are What do they eat? and Laying eggs?

options.text: subheadings that show what each part is about

options.why: What do they eat? is a question, but here it is a heading for the part below it.
They are not names.
There are no pictures in this text.

hints: Look at where these words are in the text.
Each one sits above a short part of the text.
What do the words tell you about the part below them?
items.explanation: They are subheadings. Each one tells you what the next part of the text is about, so you can find information quickly.

items.prompt: Which pair of words rhyme in the poem?

options.why: Kite and string end with different sounds.
Sky and hill end with different sounds.
Town rhymes with brown, not with sun.

hints: Rhyming words end with the same sound.
Look at the last word of each line.
Say each pair aloud. Which pair sounds the same at the end?
items.explanation: Breeze and trees both end with the same sound, so they rhyme. In this poem, each pair of lines ends with rhyming words.

items.prompt: A small red bird against the sun. What is the poet describing in this line?

options.why: A real mynah bird comes later. This line is about something red.
The sun is behind the thing being described.
The roofs are far below.

hints: What in the poem is red?
Read the lines just before this one.
What danced, dipped and swooped above the town?
items.explanation: The red kite is flying so high that it looks like a small red bird in the sky.

items.prompt: In a playscript, what are the words in brackets for?

options.text: They are words the characters say quietly.
options.why: The characters do not say the words in brackets.

options.text: They are the title of the play.
options.why: The title is at the top.

options.text: They tell the actors what to do or how to speak.
They are questions for the reader.
options.why: They are not questions.

hints: Look at (worried) and (jumping up).
Do the characters say these words out loud?
Think about what an actor needs to know to play the part.
items.explanation: Words in brackets are stage directions. They tell the actors what to do, or how to say their lines.

items.prompt: The writer wants Mrs Lim to say It's all right, Amir in a soft voice. How should it be written in the playscript?

options.text: MRS LIM: (softly) It's all right, Amir.
“It's all right, Amir,” said Mrs Lim softly.
options.why: That is how a story shows speech. Playscripts do not use speech marks.

options.text: MRS LIM: It's all right, Amir, she said softly.
options.why: Playscripts do not use said. How to speak goes in brackets.

options.text: (MRS LIM) softly: It's all right, Amir.
options.why: The name goes first with a colon, then the stage direction in brackets.

hints: Look at how the other lines in the play are written.
Where does the speaker's name go? Where does the way of speaking go?
Compare each answer with Amir's line that begins with (worried).
items.explanation: In a playscript, the name comes first, then a colon. How to speak goes in brackets before the words, and there are no speech marks.

items.prompt: Which of these would NOT belong in Bima's letter?

options.why: Letters start with a greeting.
Bima uses paragraphs to organise his news.

options.text: a sign-off, like With lots of love
options.why: Letters end with a sign-off and a name.

hints: Think about the features of a friendly letter.
Which of these would you usually see in an information text?
Look at Bima's letter. Which feature is not there?
items.explanation: A letter has an address, a date, a greeting, paragraphs and a sign-off. Subheadings belong in information texts.

items.prompt: Bima writes that the road twisted round and round like a snake. What does this tell you?

options.text: The road had lots of bends.
There were snakes on the road.
options.why: Bima is comparing the road to the shape of a snake.
The bus ride took an hour.

options.text: The road was straight and flat.
options.why: Twisted round and round means it was not straight.

hints: Picture a snake moving on the ground.
Is a snake's body straight or curvy?
The word like shows that Bima is comparing two things.
items.explanation: A snake moves in curves, so the comparison shows that the road had lots of bends.

items.prompt: Why are the steps in the instructions numbered?

options.text: to show how many pages there are
options.why: The numbers are next to the steps, not pages.

options.text: to show the order to do them in
to make the text look longer
options.why: The numbers are there to help the reader.

options.text: to count the boats you will make
options.why: You make one boat.

hints: Think about what happens if you do the steps in the wrong order.
Number 1 comes first. What comes next?
Why do recipes and instructions use numbers?
items.explanation: The numbers show the order of the steps. You must fold in the right order, or the boat will not work.

items.prompt: Why does the writer put the Top tip after the steps?

options.text: It is the most important step.
options.why: The steps make the boat. The tip helps it last longer.

options.text: The writer forgot to put it first.
options.why: It is placed at the end on purpose.

options.text: It tells you what you need.
options.why: That is the You will need list at the top.

options.text: It is extra advice, and it is not one of the folding steps.

hints: Read the Top tip again.
Do you need it to fold the boat?
When will you use the wax crayon?
items.explanation: The tip is extra advice for after the boat is folded. It is not one of the folding steps, so it goes at the end.

items.prompt: Why does the report end with Did you know?

options.text: to ask you to write an answer
options.why: It is a heading, and the answer is given below it.

options.text: to tell a story about pandas
options.why: It is one fact, not a story.

options.text: to give an extra fun fact

options.why: That is how instructions start.

hints: Read the last part of the report.
Is the panda fact about bamboo in Indonesia?
Why might a writer add something surprising at the end?
items.explanation: Did you know? introduces an extra fun fact. Reports often use a box like this to add something interesting.

items.prompt: Where do you look to find the meaning of a hard word in a book?
hints: A glossary is like a mini dictionary.
It is usually at the back.
It explains words from the book.
items.explanation: The glossary explains hard words.

options.why: The index lists topics and pages.

The title page shows the title.

hints: It is near the front of a book.
It lists parts in order.
The numbers are page numbers.
items.explanation: A contents page lists chapters and page numbers.

options.why: That is the glossary.

options.text: the chapters and where they start

options.why: It is not about the writer.
It lists chapters.

items.prompt: Which feature helps you find a topic at the back of a book?
hints: It is in alphabetical order.
It lists topics and page numbers.
It is at the back.
items.explanation: The index lists topics and pages.

options.why: The title is on the cover.
A heading is in the text.
A caption is by a picture.

hints: A caption is next to a photo or drawing.
It is short.
It tells you what you are looking at.
items.explanation: A caption explains a picture.

options.why: That is the contents page.

options.text: It gives the meaning of a word.

A caption goes with a picture.
An index helps you find pages.
items.explanation: Each feature helps the reader.
pairs: tells the topic of a part

items.prompt: Sort the parts of a book.

You see the title first.
Lists of words come at the end.
items.explanation: Cover, title page and contents are at the front. Index and glossary are at the back.

items.prompt: Some words in a text are in bold print. Why?
hints: Bold words are thicker.
The writer wants you to notice them.
They are often in the glossary.
items.explanation: Bold words are important or new words.

options.why: Bold does not show a spelling mistake.
Bold is about the look of the word.
Bold is not only for names.

items.prompt: Put the parts of an information book in order from the front.
hints: Start with the title.
The contents tell you what is inside.
The index is at the back.
items.explanation: Title page, contents, chapters, index.

items.prompt: A diagram has labels. What do the labels do?

They tell you what each part is.
